title: Kubernetes Guard Rails: Admission Policies (Kyverno) and Runtime Detection (Falco)
intro: Scanning finds problems; policy prevents them. An admission controller checks every object before the cluster accepts it, so 'no privileged pods' or 'only signed images' becomes a rule nobody can forget. Runtime detection watches what containers actually do once they're running. Kyverno and Falco are the common open-source choices.

steps.prompt: List the cluster-wide Kyverno policies and whether they block or only report.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                        ADMISSION   BACKGROUND   VALIDATE ACTION   READY
disallow-privileged         true        true         Enforce           True
require-signed-images       true        true         Enforce           True
require-resource-limits     true        true         Audit             True
steps.explanation: Two policies block violations; one only reports them.
steps.why: Enforce rejects the request; Audit lets it through and records a violation. New policies start in Audit, so you see what they'd break before they break it. A policy engine is itself an admission webhook, with the failure mode shown in incident-014: exclude its own namespace and run it with several replicas.

steps.prompt: Test the privileged-pod policy: try to run a privileged pod named hack from the alpine image.
steps.fake_output:
Error from server: admission webhook "validate.kyverno.svc-fail" denied the request:

resource Pod/default/hack was blocked due to the following policies

disallow-privileged:
  privileged-containers: 'validation error: Privileged mode is disallowed. rule privileged-containers failed at path /spec/containers/0/securityContext/privileged/'
steps.explanation: The API server refused to create the pod, and said which policy and which field.
steps.why: A privileged container has nearly full access to its node, so it's the usual route from 'compromised pod' to 'compromised cluster'. Blocking it at admission means a mistake in a manifest, or an attacker with deploy rights, can't create one. Kubernetes' built-in Pod Security Admission covers these baseline rules too (tutorial-027); Kyverno adds custom ones.

steps.prompt: Test a manifest against the policies before it reaches the cluster, in CI: apply the policy file policies/ to deployment.yaml with the Kyverno CLI.
steps.fake_output:
Applying 3 policy rule(s) to 1 resource(s)...

policy require-resource-limits -> resource default/Deployment/api failed:
  validate-limits: validation error: CPU and memory limits are required.

pass: 2, fail: 1, warn: 0, error: 0, skip: 0
steps.explanation: The manifest would violate the resource-limits policy.
steps.why: Running policies in CI gives developers the failure in their pull request, not at deploy time. The same policy files serve both places, so the rules can't drift apart.

steps.prompt: See what the audit-mode policy has caught so far across the cluster.
steps.fake_output:
NAMESPACE   NAME                        PASS   FAIL   WARN   ERROR   SKIP
shop        cpol-require-resource-limits   14     3      0      0       0
legacy      cpol-require-resource-limits   2      9      0      0       0
steps.why: Policy reports are the to-do list before switching a policy to Enforce: fix or exempt what fails, then turn enforcement on. Jumping straight to Enforce blocks the next deploy of every non-compliant workload, usually during an incident.

steps.prompt: Admission checks what is deployed; runtime detection watches behaviour. Look at Falco's recent alerts.
steps.fake_output:
10:41:02 Notice A shell was spawned in a container with an attached terminal (user=root container=checkout-5d7c8b6a4-m8n2q shell=bash parent=runc)
10:41:19 Warning Sensitive file opened for reading by non-trusted program (file=/etc/shadow command=cat /etc/shadow container=checkout-5d7c8b6a4-m8n2q)
10:42:07 Error Outbound connection to a known crypto-mining pool (connection=10.1.4.21:51876->45.9.148.3:3333 container=checkout-5d7c8b6a4-m8n2q)
steps.explanation: Someone opened a shell in a production container, read /etc/shadow, and connected to a mining pool.
steps.why: Falco watches system calls and matches them against rules, so it sees what a signed, scanned, policy-compliant image does after it's been compromised. Those three alerts in sequence are the attack in security-incident-004 and mystery-linux-005, caught as it happens. Send the alerts somewhere a person will see them; a detection nobody reads isn't one.
